title: Karan Johar Bet on Ananya Panday and Lakshya. The Box Office Said No. Chand Mera Dil Is Already a Netflix Problem.
excerpt: Dharma's latest romance opened to ₹2.75 crore. The generation that cried during K3G is watching Korean dramas now.
body:
Karan Johar's Dharma Productions has spent two decades turning unknown faces into household names. Student of the Year made Varun Dhawan and Alia Bhatt. Dhadak made Janhvi Kapoor viable. Rocky Aur Rani brought Ranveer Singh and Alia Bhatt back to the mid-week audience. The formula is proven: take a glossy aesthetic, a soundtrack you can hum in the shower, a pair of faces too beautiful to ignore, and release it on a holiday Friday.

Chand Mera Dil followed the playbook exactly. It paired Ananya Panday — still looking for her first genuine solo hit — with Lakshya, the TV actor who broke out on Splitsvilla and hasn't quite broken into film yet. The trailer was competent, the music decent, and the release date (May 22) gave it an open corridor with no major competition.

It opened to ₹2.75-3 crore on day one.

### The Numbers Tell the Story

By day two, the film had crawled to ₹6.65 crore total. The jump from Friday to Saturday — traditionally the moment word-of-mouth kicks in — was only about 21 percent. For context, Ananya's last theatrical outing, Tu Meri Main Tera Main Tera Tu Meri with Kartik Aaryan, opened at ₹7.75 crore on its first day alone. Chand Mera Dil needed its entire opening weekend to match that single-day figure.

The worldwide gross stands at roughly ₹8.19 crore after two days. There's been no dramatic upswing.

### What Went Wrong

The problem isn't Ananya Panday's screen presence or Lakshya's commitment — both do what's asked of them. The problem is that Dharma is running the 2015 playbook in a 2026 market. The romantic drama as a genre is clinically dead in Indian theatres unless it comes with either star power (Shah Rukh Khan), a gimmick (time travel, supernatural), or a director whose name alone sells tickets (Imtiaz Ali, Sanjay Leela Bhansali).

A straight love story between two people under 30 who are not yet stars simply doesn't move the needle at multiplexes anymore. It moves the needle on OTT, where the economics are different and the audience more forgiving. Every trade analyst watching Chand Mera Dil's trajectory has already started speculating about its Netflix premiere date.

### The Dharma Brand and the NRI Question

For NRIs, Dharma films have always been something else entirely. Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham defined an entire generation's relationship with missing home. Kal Ho Naa Ho made Manhattan feel like Mumbai. The Dharma aesthetic — big houses, designer saris, emotional confrontations set to A.R. Rahman or Pritam scores — was the NRI's Bollywood. You didn't need to know the actors; you needed to feel the feelings.

Chand Mera Dil aims for that same emotional register. But the generation that cried during K3G now has children who watch Korean dramas on Netflix. The generation Dharma is trying to reach — Gen Z NRIs — doesn't have the same automatic loyalty to the brand.

### What Comes Next

The film will likely end its theatrical run in the ₹20-25 crore range in India. Netflix reportedly holds the digital rights, and a streaming premiere in late June or July is expected. That's where it might actually find its audience — people who'll stumble across it on a Saturday night, watch it in bed, and think it was perfectly fine.

Perfectly fine. That's the distance between 2026 Dharma and the Dharma that once made an entire diaspora weep in IMAX.
author: Diaspora Desk
